# Chapter 6 — Managed Identity Governance

## System-Assigned vs. User-Assigned Governance Posture

Managed identities represent the operationally cleanest form of Azure workload authentication, precisely because they eliminate the credential management burden that makes app registrations difficult to govern: there are no client secrets to rotate, no certificates to renew, no credentials to store in application configuration files or key vaults. The Azure fabric handles the cryptographic lifecycle entirely. For governance purposes, however, managed identities present a different kind of challenge — not credential drift, but permission drift. Managed identities accumulate Azure RBAC role assignments over the lifetime of the workload they serve, and those role assignments are not automatically reviewed or revoked when the workload's requirements change. A managed identity for a data pipeline workload that originally needed Storage Blob Data Contributor on a single storage account may have accumulated additional role assignments as the pipeline expanded, and when the pipeline was retired, the managed identity and all its role assignments may have been left in place.

System-assigned managed identities have a natural lifecycle anchor: they are created and deleted with the Azure resource they are attached to. When the virtual machine or App Service instance is deprovisioned, the managed identity is deprovisioned with it, and all its RBAC role assignments become orphaned role assignments at the scope they were made — role assignments referencing a deleted principal, which Azure RBAC reports as unknown principals. The governance model for system-assigned managed identities focuses primarily on role assignment hygiene during the resource's operational lifetime, and on ensuring that the Azure Policy tagging framework established in Part Five correctly places the resource — and therefore the managed identity — in the organizational hierarchy. The OrgPath tag on the resource is the governance anchor for the system-assigned managed identity; no separate attribute-writing step is needed.

User-assigned managed identities are substantially more complex. They are independent Azure resource objects — created in a resource group, assigned a resource group and subscription scope, tagged separately from any compute resource they are attached to — and they persist independently of any specific workload. A user-assigned managed identity originally created for a container application that has since been replaced may still exist in the resource group, may still hold RBAC role assignments, and may even still be attached to infrastructure that was repurposed rather than deprovisioned. The governance model for user-assigned managed identities requires explicit OrgPath tagging, enforced through Azure Policy, and inclusion in the drift detection pipeline that checks OrgPath validity against the OrgTree registry.

## Azure Policy Enforcement for User-Assigned Managed Identity Tagging

The tagging policy for user-assigned managed identities follows the same pattern as the Arc resource tagging policy established in Part Five. The policy targets the Microsoft.ManagedIdentity/userAssignedIdentities resource type and requires that all four OrgPath governance tags — OrgPath, OrgNodeId, OrgTier, and MigrationPhase — be present at creation time. The effect is deny: any create or update operation on a user-assigned managed identity that omits any of the four tags is rejected at the Azure Resource Manager layer before the resource is created. The policy is assigned at the management group level to apply uniformly across all subscriptions in the organizational hierarchy, consistent with the governance posture of the broader OrgPath substrate.

## Policy 6.1 — Azure Policy: Require OrgPath Tags on User-Assigned Managed Identities (JSON)

```json
{
  "properties": {
    "displayName": "OrgPath — Require governance tags on User-Assigned Managed Identities",
    "description": "Denies creation of user-assigned managed identities that do not carry all four OrgPath governance tags.",
    "mode": "Indexed",
    "parameters": {},
    "policyRule": {
      "if": {
        "allOf": [
          {
            "field": "type",
            "equals": "Microsoft.ManagedIdentity/userAssignedIdentities"
          },
          {
            "anyOf": [
              { "field": "tags['OrgPath']",       "exists": "false" },
              { "field": "tags['OrgNodeId']",      "exists": "false" },
              { "field": "tags['OrgTier']",        "exists": "false" },
              { "field": "tags['MigrationPhase']", "exists": "false" }
            ]
          }
        ]
      },
      "then": {
        "effect": "deny"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

## Managed Identity Drift Detection

The drift detection scope in the pipeline established in Chapter Five should be extended to include user-assigned managed identities. The extension reads all user-assigned managed identities from the Azure Resource Manager API, checks the OrgPath tag value against the active nodes in the OrgTree registry, and adds any findings to the drift report. Because the Azure Policy enforces tag presence at creation time, the only sources of drift for managed identities created after the policy was assigned are OrgPath values referencing nodes that were subsequently archived or removed from the OrgTree. For managed identities created before the policy was assigned — legacy identities that predate the governance framework — the Phase Zero inventory and triage process applies in the same way as it does for app registrations: inventory, triage, tag-stamp, verify. The policy assignment combined with the drift detection pipeline maintains a closed-loop governance posture going forward: no new untagged managed identity can be created, and existing tagged identities whose OrgPath becomes invalid are detected in the next drift run and surfaced for remediation.

::: {.callout-note title="Operational Note: RBAC Role Assignment Audit for Managed Identities"}
The drift detection pipeline for managed identities should be extended to emit the role assignments held by each managed identity alongside its OrgPath validity status. A managed identity with a valid OrgPath and appropriate role assignments requires no action. A managed identity with a valid OrgPath and role assignments at a subscription scope broader than expected — for example, a Contributor role at the subscription level for a managed identity that should have storage-scoped access only — should be surfaced as a permission drift finding. The Get-AzRoleAssignment -ObjectId &lt;ManagedIdentityObjectId&gt; call produces this information and can be added to the drift report output with minimal pipeline modification.
:::
